At dawn, the town woke beneath a sky the color of unpolished silver. The bakery opened first, breathing warm yeast into the narrow street. Then came the fishmonger, dragging his blue awning across the pavement, and the woman who sold buttons from a velvet case. Nobody noticed the small door appearing between the pharmacy and the shuttered cinema. It had no handle, no frame, and no sign. It was simply a rectangle of dark green painted upon brick. A cat sat before it, watching passersby with the solemn patience of a guard who had forgotten the name of the kingdom.

Mara saw the door on her way to work. She was late, as usual, carrying a paper cup of coffee that had already cooled. She paused because the cat was orange, and because its left ear was folded like a torn page. When she crouched, it touched its nose to the green paint. The door opened inward without a sound. Beyond it lay not a room but a summer field, bright with grass and yellow flowers. Wind moved through it in long waves. Mara smelled rain, though the town had not seen rain for three weeks. Behind her, someone cleared his throat.

“Are you coming?” said a voice behind her. Mara turned and found Mr Vale, the retired postman, holding his bicycle by one rusted handlebar. He wore his usual gray cap and an expression of private weather. “That door was here yesterday,” he said. “But yesterday it opened onto the sea.” Mara looked again. The field had vanished. In its place rolled a dark shore beneath gulls that made no noise. Far away, a lighthouse blinked once, twice, then not at all. “Where does it go?” Mara asked. Mr Vale shrugged. “Wherever it is needed, perhaps. Or wherever it is hungry.”

Mara should have gone to the office, where invoices waited in neat accusing stacks. Instead she stepped through. The cat followed, its tail raised like a question. At once the town disappeared behind her, although she could still hear a bus sighing at a curb. The grass bent beneath her shoes, wet and cool. She walked toward the lighthouse because there was nothing else to do. Halfway across the field, she found a table laid for breakfast. There were two cups, a pot of tea, and a bowl full of blackberries. A note rested beside the spoon. It read, “Wait.”

She did not wait. This was not bravery, exactly, nor impatience. It was the practical instinct of someone who had spent years answering other people’s messages before they became emergencies. Mara poured tea into one cup and drank it while walking. The tea tasted of mint, smoke, and a memory she could not place. At the lighthouse door, she found a child sitting on the steps. He wore a red raincoat despite sun. “My mother went in,” he said. “She has been gone for a year.” Mara looked at the door. It was painted the same dark green. “Then we go.”

Inside, the lighthouse contained a staircase that circled downward instead of up. The walls were lined with postcards, thousands of them, each showing a place Mara had never visited. A desert with purple shadows. A city built on stilts above clouds. A kitchen where an old woman laughed beside a stove. The child ran ahead, calling “Mother?” into the turning dark. No answer came, but postcard fluttered loose and landed at Mara’s feet. It showed the town square under snow. On the back, someone had written, “Please remember the people who wait for you.” Mara folded it. The cat sneezed.

At the bottom of the staircase, they entered a station. Trains stood along three platforms, but none had wheels. Their windows showed different weather: snow, lightning, falling leaves, a sunset green as copper. The child walked to the carriage and pressed his palm against its glass. On the other side, a woman in a red coat lifted her hand. Her face was blurred, as if seen through water. “That is her,” the child whispered. “Why cannot she come out?” Mr Vale, who had followed them, pointed to a clock above the platform. Its hands moved backward. “Because someone must choose.”

Mara understood nothing, which was perhaps why she understood enough. She remembered the note, the postcards, the field waiting patiently behind impossible doors. “What do I choose?” she asked. Mr Vale looked suddenly older than his gray cap, older than the town, older than the lighthouse. “You choose whether you will carry what you have seen back with you,” he said. “Most people leave it here. That is why the world becomes so forgetful.” Mara looked at the child, at the woman beyond the glass, and at the cat washing one white paw. “I choose to remember them.”

The station lights went out. For one breath, Mara felt herself become a postcard, flat and weightless, carried by unknown hands. Then every train window blazed open. Rain poured through one. Sand streamed through another. From the carriage beside the child, his mother stepped onto the platform, older only by tears. She knelt and held him so tightly that Mara looked away. The clock stopped. Somewhere above, the lighthouse began to ring, although it had no bell. Mr Vale smiled beneath his cap. “Now,” he said, “run. Your office will be wondering where you are.” Mara laughed. It surprised her greatly.

She ran upward, though the stairs seemed to descend. The cat raced beside her, then vanished through a crack in the wall, perhaps returning to its ordinary duties. Mara emerged into the street with her coffee in one hand. The green door was gone. The bakery breathed cinnamon. A bus sighed at the curb. Snow began to fall, soft and improbable, over the morning. Across the square, Mr Vale pedaled past on his bicycle, delivering letters with care. Mara went to work. She answered invoices, called suppliers, and apologized for being late. But that evening, she remembered everything.
